newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom may be opening up to foreign investors - WSJ.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom may be opening up to foreign investors - WSJ.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly Gazprom is encouraging foreign investment in its domestic shares in a move that could have sweeping implications for the market, the Wall Street Journal Europe said on Thursday.
"We think that if a company is registered here, it has rights equal to the rights of any investor," the newspaper quoted Gazprom Chairman Rem Vyakhirev as saying in an interview.
It added that Vyakhirev's comments appeared to be the first time that he had stated publicly that foreigners can buy the company's coveted shares within Russia.
The Journal said Vyakhirev acknowledged that many of the foreign companies in Russia which buy Gazprom stock were "front companies" operating on behalf of clients abroad.
But he warned, "You cannot transfer the shares, only the profits" to outside investors. "You can buy as much as 60 percent," he said. "But you have to trade them here."

Vyakhirev's comments followed a bitter controversy involving an international fund company which backed down from plans to invest in the domestic shares of Gazprom in the face of stiff opposition from the corporation.

Regent Gaz Investment Co Ltd had been planning to take advantage of the fact that internationally traded shares in Gazprom, quoted in the form of American Depositary Shares in London, cost about four times as much as Gazprom shares in Russia.
"They simply violated our procedure for the sale of shares and accordingly decreased the value of the company," Vyakhirev told the Wall Street Journal. "They inflicted damage on us."

The paper described the remarks as "a stunning display of openness" with sweeping implications for foreigners who hope to get a piece of the action in Russia and for the Russian economy. Potential buyers of Gazprom shares in Russia are wary of restrictions on foreign ownership.

It quoted analysts as saying this was the first time Vyakhirev had invited foreigners into the domestic market and that his remarks "left little doubt that foreigners could now participate locally without asking Gazprom's permission -- even when they are representing stockholders abroad".
No immediate comment was available from Gazprom in Moscow.
